# Document structure and formatting {short-title="Structure"}

This chapter presents the basic building blocks of any Quarto document: heading hierarchy,
numbering, section cross-references, and inline formatting.

## Heading hierarchy {#sec-headings}

Quarto supports four levels of numbered headings in this template (parameter
`number-depth: 4` in `_extension.yml`). The syntax uses Markdown hashes:

````markdown
# Chapter heading (level 1)

## Section heading (level 2)

### Subsection heading (level 3)

#### Sub-subsection heading (level 4)
````

In PDF, these levels correspond respectively to the LaTeX commands `\chapter`,
`\section`, `\subsection`, and `\subsubsection`. In HTML, they generate the tags
`<h2>` through `<h5>` (with `<h1>` reserved for the book title).

### Demonstration subsection {#sec-demo-subsection}

This is a `###` in context. The automatic numbering produces "1.1.1" here.

#### Demonstration sub-subsection

And this is a `####`, numbered "1.1.1.1". Beyond this level, Quarto stops numbering —
use lists or bold paragraphs if you need a fifth level.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Recommended maximum depth

A four-level numbered outline is generally the maximum acceptable in a thesis. A deeper
outline is often a sign that the structure needs rethinking.
:::

## Numbered and unnumbered sections {#sec-numbering}

By default, all headings from level 1 to 4 are numbered. To remove the numbering, add
the class `{.unnumbered}`:

````markdown
## Section without number {.unnumbered}
````

For front matter and back matter pages (acknowledgements, abstract, conclusion…), combine
`{.unnumbered}` with `{.toc-black}` — the latter class instructs the Lua filter to display
the title in black in the table of contents, and triggers roman numeral page numbering in
the front matter when `pagestyle-sections: true`:

````markdown
# Conclusion {.unnumbered}

# Acknowledgements {.unnumbered .toc-black}
````

::: {.callout-important}
## `.unnumbered` vs `.unnumbered .toc-black`

- `{.unnumbered}` alone: unnumbered heading, displayed in colour in the {{< acrs toc >}}
  (chapters in the thesis body: introduction, conclusion).
- `{.unnumbered .toc-black}`: unnumbered heading, displayed in **black** in the
  {{< acrs toc >}} (front matter and back matter sections).

Never put `{.unnumbered}` on a numbered body chapter (chapters 1, 2, 3…) — it would be
inconsistent with the overall structure.
:::

## Section cross-references (`@sec-`) {#sec-crossref}

To create a cross-reference to a section, you need to: (1) give an identifier to the
target heading with `{#sec-label}`, then (2) reference it with `@sec-label`:

````markdown
## Heading hierarchy {#sec-headings}

As explained in @sec-headings, levels range from `#` to `####`.
````

::: {.render-demo}
**Output:**

As explained in @sec-headings, levels range from `#` to `####`.
:::

Quarto automatically resolves the number and hyperlink in both formats.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Label naming convention

Use the prefix `sec-` for sections, `fig-` for figures, `tbl-` for tables, `eq-` for
equations. These prefixes are required by Quarto for cross-references to work correctly
in both output formats.
:::

## Short title (`short-title`) {#sec-short-title}

When a chapter or section title is too long to fit in the PDF running header or in the
table of contents, use the `short-title` attribute:

````markdown
# A really very long title that overflows into the header {short-title="Short title"}

## A subsection with an extremely long title {short-title="Short title"}
````

The short title is used in the running header (recto/verso page header) and in the table
of contents. The long title remains unchanged in the body of the text.

::: {.callout-tip}
Aim for 40 to 50 characters maximum for a `short-title`. Beyond that, it may also
overflow depending on the layout.
:::

## Inline formatting {#sec-inline}

### Emphasis and code

````markdown
**bold**, *italic*, ***bold italic***, `inline code`
~~strikethrough~~, ^superscript^, ~subscript~
:::
````

::: {.render-demo}
**Output:**

**bold**, *italic*, ***bold italic***, `inline code`,
~~strikethrough~~, ^superscript^, ~subscript~.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Academic use of bold and italic

In a thesis, bold and italic serve to mark **terminology** at first introduction, or to
cite a *book title*. Using them to decorate text or emphasise entire sentences is a
practice to avoid.
:::

### Underline

Markdown has no native syntax for underlining. Quarto uses the span notation with the
`.underline` class:

````markdown
[underlined text]{.underline}
````

::: {.render-demo}
**Output:** [underlined text]{.underline}.
:::

In PDF, Pandoc generates `\underline{…}`; in HTML, a `<span>` with
`text-decoration: underline`. The `<u>text</u>` syntax works in HTML but is ignored
in PDF.

::: {.callout-caution}
## Underlining should be avoided in a thesis

Underlining is a legacy of the typewriter era, when italic was not available. In a
typeset document, it is reserved for hyperlinks. To highlight a term, use `*italic*`
or `**bold**`.
:::

### Lists {#sec-lists}

````markdown
- First unordered item
- Second item
  - Sub-item (2-space indentation)

1. First ordered item
1. Second item
   a. Sub-item (3-space indentation)
````

::: {.render-demo}
**Output:**

- First unordered item
- Second item
  - Sub-item (2-space indentation)

1. First ordered item
1. Second item
   a. Sub-item (3-space indentation)
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## The written number does not matter

Pandoc only reads the number of the **first** item (to determine the counter start);
all subsequent numbers are ignored and auto-incremented. These two syntaxes produce
the same output:

```markdown
1. First
2. Second
3. Third
```

```markdown
1. First
1. Second
1. Third
```

The `1. 1. 1.` convention is even recommended: no need to renumber if an item is
inserted or moved. The same logic applies to sub-lists: `a. a. a.` is sufficient
to obtain `a.`, `b.`, `c.`…
:::


### Task lists {#sec-tasklists}

The `- [ ]` / `- [x]` syntax produces a task list. The case of `x` does not matter
(`X` works too):

````markdown
- [ ] Write the introduction
- [x] Choose the Quarto template
- [ ] Submit to the thesis supervisor
````

::: {.render-demo}
**Output:**

- [ ] Write the introduction
- [x] Choose the Quarto template
- [ ] Submit to the thesis supervisor
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Different rendering depending on the output format

In **HTML**, Quarto generates real `<input type="checkbox">` elements (disabled,
non-interactive).

In **PDF** (pdflatex), Pandoc uses the mathematical symbols `$\square$` (empty box)
and `$\boxtimes$` (checked box) from the `amssymb` package. The appearance is correct
but typographically different from HTML checkboxes.
:::

::: {.callout-caution}
## Use in a thesis

Task lists are suited to working notes, methodological appendices, or a README. In
the thesis body, prefer a plain unordered list accompanied by a state verb ("completed",
"in progress"…): it is more neutral and more consistent with academic register.
:::

### Blockquotes

````markdown
> "Typography is the craft of endowing human language with a durable visual form."
>
> — Robert Bringhurst [@Bringhurst2004]
````

::: {.render-demo}
**Output:**

> "Typography is the craft of endowing human language with a durable visual form."
>
> — Robert Bringhurst [@Bringhurst2004]
:::

::: {.callout-caution}
## Definition lists in pdflatex

Pandoc's definition list syntax (`term\n:  definition`) is supported by Quarto but
produces no particular visual style in pdflatex. If you need formatted definition
lists, use a Markdown table (see @sec-tables-simple) or a raw LaTeX environment.
:::

### Footnotes {#sec-footnotes}

Quarto offers two syntaxes for footnotes.

**Inline syntax** — the note is written directly in the text, between `^[` and `]`:

````markdown
The Cnam was founded in 1794^[Decree of the National Convention of 19 Vendémiaire
Year III (10 October 1794).] on the initiative of Abbé Grégoire.
````

::: {.render-demo}
**Output:**

The Cnam was founded in 1794^[Decree of the National Convention of 19 Vendémiaire
Year III (10 October 1794).] on the initiative of Abbé Grégoire.
:::

**Reference syntax** — the footnote call and its content are separated. Useful for
long notes or to keep the main text readable:

````markdown
The thesis must be deposited on theses.fr[^deposit] before the defence.

[^deposit]: National thesis portal managed by the {{< acrs abes >}},
    accessible at <https://theses.fr>.
````

::: {.render-demo}
**Output:**

The thesis must be deposited on theses.fr[^deposit] before the defence.

[^deposit]: National thesis portal managed by the {{< acrs abes >}},
    accessible at <https://theses.fr>.
:::

In PDF, both syntaxes produce a numbered footnote at the bottom of the page. In HTML,
they produce an interactive footnote (clickable number with a back-reference to the
call site).

::: {.callout-tip}
## Which syntax to choose?

Prefer the **inline syntax** `^[…]` for short notes (one sentence) — the content
remains visible while writing. Use the **reference syntax** `[^label]` for long or
multi-paragraph notes, and to avoid visually cluttering the Markdown source when the
note exceeds two lines.
:::

### Page breaks {#sec-pagebreak}

Quarto provides the `{{< pagebreak >}}` shortcode to insert a page break compatible
with both output formats:

````markdown
End of this section's content.

{{</* pagebreak */>}}

Start of the next section.
````

In PDF, `{{< pagebreak >}}` generates `\newpage`. In HTML, it inserts a
`page-break-after: always` style rule — with no visible effect on screen, but useful
if the HTML page is printed from the browser.

::: {.callout-tip}
## `\newpage` vs `\clearpage`

If you need `\clearpage` (flushes pending floats before jumping) rather than
`\newpage`, use a raw LaTeX block inside a `{.content-visible when-format="pdf"}`:

````markdown
::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
```{=latex}
\clearpage
```
:::
````

In a thesis with many figures, `\clearpage` is often preferable to prevent floats
from accumulating and appearing well after their insertion point in the text.
:::

::: {.callout-caution}
## Manual page breaks should be used sparingly

As a general rule, let LaTeX manage the layout. Manual page breaks solve a local
problem but can create others further on in the document (blank pages, displaced
floats). Prefer to adjust them at the very end of writing, once the content is fixed.
:::
